abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is frequently accompanied by anorexia, cachexia, and inflammation, which collectively contribute to poor clinical outcomes. However, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here we demonstrate a pivotal role for growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) in CKD morbidities. Deteriorating renal function and clinical disease status correlates with GDF15 levels in plasma and kidneys of CKD patients. In a mouse CKD model, GDF15 levels are elevated and Gdf15 knockout (Gdf15-/-) mice are partially protected from CKD-induced anorexia and weight loss despite worsening renal function and inflammation. GDF15 receptor Gfral knockout (Gfral-/-) mice recapitulate these phenotypes. Metabolic cage studies reveal that the weight loss-protection effects are primarily attributed to increased food intake. Intriguingly, pair-fed Gdf15-/- and Gfral-/- mice exhibited phenotypic and molecular divergence. Pair feeding in Gdf15-/- mice reverses loss-of-GDF15's effect on body weight but does not restore renal functions. In contrast, pair feeding in Gfral-/- mice reverses loss-of-GFRAL's effect on both body weight and renal function. Transcriptome analysis suggests that GDF15 may act through both GFRAL-dependent mechanisms on food intake and GFRAL-independent mechanisms that primarily modulate inflammation and metabolic pathways. A monoclonal antibody that neutralizes circulating GDF15 markedly restores food intake and preserves body weight, demonstrating the therapeutic potential of targeting GDF15 in CKD-associated weight loss. Together, these findings demonstrate GDF15-GFRAL as a potential therapeutic target for CKD-associated weight loss and suggest GFRAL-dependent, food intake-mediated actions of GDF15 and food intake-independent effects that may contribute to renal inflammation and metabolic regulation.
